title: Dimensions
notes:
Fundamental Physical Quantities and Their Dimensions

In the International System of Units (SI), there are seven fundamental physical quantities, each representing an independent dimension. All other physical quantities are derived from these fundamentals. The symbols used for dimensions are enclosed in square brackets: Mass [M], Length [L], Time [T], Electric current [I] (or [A]), Temperature [K] (or [\theta]), Amount of substance [N], and Luminous intensity [J]. A dimensional formula expresses a derived quantity as a product of powers of these fundamental dimensions, e.g., [Force] = [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}].

Dimensional Formulae of Common Physical Quantities

Key derived quantities and their dimensional formulae: Velocity v = displacement/time → [M^0 L^1 T^{-1}]. Acceleration a = change in velocity/time → [M^0 L^1 T^{-2}]. Momentum p = mass × velocity → [M^1 L^1 T^{-1}]. Force F = mass × acceleration → [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]; SI unit: Newton (N) = kg·m/s². Work/Energy W = force × distance → [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]; SI unit: Joule (J). Power P = work/time → [M^1 L^2 T^{-3}]; SI unit: Watt (W) = J/s. Density \rho = mass/volume → [M^1 L^{-3} T^0]. Pressure/Stress P = force/area → [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]; SI unit: Pascal (Pa). Surface tension T = force/length → [M^1 L^0 T^{-2}]. Viscosity \eta = F/(A·dv/dx) → [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-1}].

More Derived Quantities and Their Dimensions

Gravitational constant G from F = GMm/r² → [G] = [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]. Specific heat s = Q/(m\Delta T) → [M^0 L^2 T^{-2} K^{-1}]. Thermal conductivity k = Qx/(A\Delta T·t) → [M^1 L^1 T^{-3} K^{-1}]. Modulus of elasticity Y = stress/strain → [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]. Moment of inertia I = mass × distance² → [M^1 L^2 T^0]. Angular velocity \omega = angle/time → [M^0 L^0 T^{-1}]. Angular momentum L = mvr → [M^1 L^2 T^{-1}]. Torque \tau = r × F → [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]. Frequency f = 1/T → [M^0 L^0 T^{-1}]. Angle \theta = arc/radius → [M^0 L^0 T^0] (dimensionless). Strain \epsilon = \Delta L/L → [M^0 L^0 T^0] (dimensionless).

Dimensionless Quantities

Some physical quantities have no dimensions — they are pure numbers. These include: angle (ratio of two lengths), strain (ratio of change in length to original length), refractive index (ratio of two velocities), specific gravity (ratio of two densities), coefficient of friction (ratio of two forces), Poisson's ratio (ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain), dielectric constant (ratio of capacitance with and without dielectric), solubility (mass ratio), and dissipation factor. Although dimensionless, some (like angle) carry units such as radian or degree; others (like Reynolds number) are combinations of dimensional quantities that cancel out.

Principle of Homogeneity of Dimensions

The principle of homogeneity of dimensions states: 「In a physically correct equation, the dimensions of each term on both sides must be identical.」 This follows from the fact that only quantities of the same type (same dimensions) can be added or subtracted. For example, in the equation s = ut + ½at²: [s] = [L], [ut] = [LT^{-1}][T] = [L], [½at²] = [LT^{-2}][T²] = [L]. All terms have dimension [L], so the equation is dimensionally consistent. This principle is NOT limited to addition — it applies to any equation where physical quantities are equated.

Applications of Dimensional Analysis

Dimensional analysis has three primary applications: (1) Checking dimensional consistency of equations — if LHS and RHS dimensions differ, the equation is definitely wrong (though correct dimensions don't guarantee the equation is right). (2) Deriving relations between physical quantities — if a quantity depends on others, assume a power-law form and solve for exponents (limited to at most 3 unknown exponents). (3) Converting units between systems — since the numerical value times the unit equals the physical quantity, n₁[u₁] = n₂[u₂], so n₂ = n₁ × ([u₁]/[u₂]).

Converting Units Between Systems

To convert a physical quantity from system 1 to system 2: If a quantity has dimensions [M^a L^b T^c] and its value is n₁ in system 1 with fundamental units M₁, L₁, T₁, then its value n₂ in system 2 with units M₂, L₂, T₂ is given by: n₂ = n₁ × (M₁/M₂)^a × (L₁/L₂)^b × (T₁/T₂)^c. Example: Convert 1 Newton to dyne. [F] = [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]. n₂ = 1 × (1 kg/1 g)^1 × (1 m/1 cm)^1 × (1 s/1 s)^{-2} = 10³ × 10² × 1 = 10⁵ dyne.

Limitations of Dimensional Analysis

Dimensional analysis has important limitations: (1) It cannot determine dimensionless constants (numerical factors like ½, π, 2π) — these must come from experiment or deeper theory. (2) It fails for equations involving exponential, logarithmic, or trigonometric functions — arguments of these functions must be dimensionless, but the method cannot derive them. (3) It cannot handle equations with more than three unknown dimensions (three equations, three unknowns). (4) It does not distinguish between scalar and vector quantities — both have the same dimensional formula. (5) It cannot verify whether an equation is dimensionally correct but physically wrong — e.g., s = ut + at² is dimensionally consistent but physically incorrect (missing ½).
confusion: Dimensions are NOT the same as units — [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}] is the dimension of force, but the unit can be Newton (SI) or dyne (CGS); a quantity has one unique dimensional formula but multiple possible units.

Dimensional consistency does NOT guarantee physical correctness — An equation like s = ut + at² is dimensionally correct (all terms have [L]) but the factor ½ is missing; dimensional analysis cannot detect numerical constants.

Trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions require dimensionless arguments — You cannot write sin([M L T^{-2}]); the argument must be dimensionless, so dimensional analysis cannot derive formulas involving these functions.

Having the same dimensions does NOT mean quantities are the same physical quantity — Work (ML²T^{-2}) and torque (ML²T^{-2}) share dimensions but are fundamentally different; work is a scalar, torque is a vector.

Dimensionless quantities CAN have units — Angle has dimensions [M^0 L^0 T^0] but is measured in radians; frequency has dimensions [T^{-1}] but is measured in hertz (Hz) — units are conventions, dimensions are physical properties.

You cannot add or subtract quantities with different dimensions — s = v + at is WRONG because [v] = [LT^{-1}] but [at] = [LT^{-2}][T] = [LT^{-1}]; wait, that IS correct. A better wrong example: s = vt + ½at is dimensionally inconsistent because [½at] = [LT^{-2}][T] = [LT^{-1}] ≠ [L].
Planck's constant has dimensions of angular momentum — [h] = [E/\nu] = [ML²T^{-2}]/[T^{-1}] = [ML²T^{-1}], same as [L] = [mvr]; this is why h appears in quantum conditions like L = nh/(2\pi).

Refractive index and specific gravity are both dimensionless but have different PHYSICAL meanings — Refractive index is a ratio of velocities (c/v); specific gravity is a ratio of densities. Never confuse the concepts even though both are dimensionless.
practice: Check the dimensional correctness of the equation: T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/g}, where T is time period, m is mass, g is acceleration due to gravity. [Solution: LHS [T] = [T]; RHS [2\pi]\sqrt{[M]/[LT^{-2}]} = \sqrt{[ML^{-1}T^{2}]} = [M^{1/2}L^{-1/2}T^{1}] \neq [T]. The equation is dimensionally INCORRECT. Correct form: T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g} for a simple pendulum.]
Find the dimensional formula of gravitational constant G using Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². [Solution: [G] = [F][r²]/[m₁][m₂] = [MLT^{-2}][L²]/[M][M] = [M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}].]

If the unit of length is chosen as 1 light-year (9.46 × 10¹⁵ m), the unit of time as 1 year (3.156 × 10⁷ s), and the unit of mass as 1 solar mass (2 × 10³⁰ kg), find the value of 1 m/s² in this system. [Solution: [a] = [M^0 L^1 T^{-2}]. New value = 1 × (9.46 × 10¹⁵)^{-1} × (3.156 × 10⁷)^{2} = 1.05 × 10^{-5} light-year/year².]

The velocity v of water waves may depend on wavelength \lambda, density \rho of water, and acceleration due to gravity g. Derive the formula for v using dimensional analysis. [Solution: Assume v = k\lambda^a \rho^b g^c. [LT^{-1}] = [L]^a [ML^{-3}]^b [LT^{-2}]^c. Equating: M: b=0; L: a - 3b + c = 1; T: -2c = -1 ⇒ c = ½, a = ½. So v = k\sqrt{\lambda g}. (k is dimensionless constant found experimentally.)]
Convert 1 Joule to ergs using dimensional analysis. [Solution: [W] = [ML²T^{-2}]. 1 J = 1 × (1 kg/1 g)^1 × (1 m/1 cm)^2 × (1 s/1 s)^{-2} = 10³ × 10² = 10⁷ erg.]

Check whether the equation s = u + ½a(2n-1) (distance in nth second) is dimensionally correct. [Solution: [s] = [L]; [u] = [LT^{-1}]; [a(2n-1)] = [LT^{-2}][T] = [LT^{-1}]. Wait: 2n-1 is dimensionless (n is number of seconds, a pure number). So [½a(2n-1)] = [LT^{-2}] which ≠ [LT^{-1}]. CORRECT: The equation should be s_n = u + ½a(2n-1) where s_n is distance in nth second having dimension [L], but u and a must carry appropriate dimensions. Actually: s_n = u + ½a(2n-1) means u here is initial velocity [LT^{-1}] and a(2n-1) gives [LT^{-2}][T] = [LT^{-1}] when n is in seconds. The equation IS dimensionally correct if n represents time interval.]

If force F, velocity V, and time T are taken as fundamental quantities, find the dimensions of mass and surface tension. [Solution: Since [F] = [MLT^{-2}], [M] = [F][L^{-1}][T^{2}] = [F][V^{-1}][T^{2}] = [FTV^{-1}]. Surface tension [T_s] = [MT^{-2}] = [FTV^{-1}][T^{-2}] = [FV^{-1}T^{-1}].]

The time period T of a satellite depends on gravitational constant G, mass of Earth M, and radius r. Use dimensional analysis to find the relation. [Solution: Assume T = kG^a M^b r^c. [T] = [M^{-a}L^{3a}T^{-2a}][M^b][L^c] = [M^{b-a}L^{3a+c}T^{-2a}]. Equating: b-a=0, 3a+c=0, -2a=1. So a = -½, b = -½, c = 3/2. T = k \sqrt{r^3/(GM)} (Kepler's third law, k = 2\pi).]

If energy E, velocity V, and time T are chosen as fundamental quantities, find the dimensions of mass. [Solution: [E] = [ML²T^{-2}], so [M] = [E][L^{-2}][T^{2}] = [E][V^{-2}][T^{2}] = [EV^{-2}T^{2}].]

Show that the dimensional formula of Planck's constant h is [ML²T^{-1}]. [Solution: From E = h\nu (Planck's equation), [h] = [E]/[\nu] = [ML²T^{-2}]/[T^{-1}] = [ML²T^{-1}]. This is identical to angular momentum [mvr] = [M][LT^{-1}][L] = [ML²T^{-1}], which is why h appears in quantum mechanics as the quantum of angular momentum.
universalFacts: Joseph Fourier introduced the systematic use of dimensions in 1822 in his "The Analytical Theory of Heat" — Before this, equations were checked by substituting units; Fourier realized dimensions could be treated algebraically, making it a powerful tool for discovering physical relationships.

The International System of Units (SI) was established in 1960 and defines exactly seven base quantities — meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount), candela (luminous intensity). All 200+ derived units in physics trace back to these seven through dimensional multiplication/division.

Buckingham's \pi Theorem (1914) formalized dimensional analysis — It states that an equation involving n variables and k fundamental dimensions can be rewritten as a relationship between (n-k) independent dimensionless groups (\pi terms). This is the foundation of scale modeling, fluid dynamics (Reynolds number), and aerodynamics testing.

NEB exam tip: Dimensional analysis questions commonly ask you to derive the period of a pendulum or check equation correctness — Always state the assumed formula (e.g., T = k \cdot l^a \cdot g^b), write dimensions of each term, solve the simultaneous equations, and comment on what the method CANNOT find (dimensionless constant k).

Planck's constant has the same dimensions as angular momentum — This is not coincidental; in Bohr's model, electron orbits are quantized so that angular momentum L = n\hbar = nh/(2\pi). This connection between dimensions of h and L is why quantum mechanics revolutionized atomic physics.

Speed of light c relates three fundamental dimensions — c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}, so [c] = [L][T^{-1}] = [M^{-1}L^{-3}T^{4}I^{2}]^{-1/2}[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^{4}I^{2}]^{-1/2}, linking mechanics [L,T] to electromagnetism [M,I]. This unification by Maxwell predicted light as an electromagnetic wave.

When solving dimensional analysis problems, remember: angles and pure numbers are dimensionless — In formulas like \theta = \omega t or \sin\theta, the angle \theta has dimension [M^0 L^0 T^0]. Don't include angle in your dimensional balance equations; treat it as having no dimensions.
